title: How Beauty Brands Use Volume Discounts to Reduce Churn Without Killing Margins | skio
summary: Grow basket size and keep beauty subscribers longer by swapping flat discounts for cart-value tiers priced against true COGS, with the margin math to prove it.
body_markdown:
Most beauty brands set their subscription discount once, usually somewhere between 10% and 15% off, and never touch it again. It’s easy to set up. It’s also quietly expensive.


A flat discount treats a $30 single-item subscriber exactly the same as a $120 subscriber buying four products. One of those customers is far more likely to stick around, and your pricing does nothing to create more of them.


**Volume discounts on subscriptions lift beauty brand LTV by rewarding customers who buy more SKUs per order, which reduces churn and per-order shipping costs at the same time.** This post covers how to structure them, the margin math, and how to test without blowing up your P&L. For the broader playbook, see our[complete guide to volume discounts for subscriptions](https://skio.com/blog/volume-discounts-that-drive-subscription-aov-a-complete-guide) .


## Why flat subscription discounts leave money on the table


Flat discounts don’t push anyone to add a second product. They don’t create a reason to stay at the moment a subscriber is deciding whether to cancel. And they hand the same margin to your lowest-value subscribers as to your best ones.


Beauty makes this worse, because beauty customers behave in two very different ways. A beauty brand leader put it bluntly on a call with us.


> Subscription for us is, like, 10% of revenue. We are not like a groom’s or a consumable where, like, we default. Especially because people are so disloyal in the beauty space. I either they are hyper loyal to one product and and not the rest of the brand, or they are trying everything under the sun.


That split is the whole problem. Single-product subscribers are fragile, since one bad experience with that one product ends the relationship. Experimenters bounce between brands. A flat discount does nothing for either group.


**Flat subscription discounts don’t differentiate between high-value multi-product subscribers and single-item churners, which leaves LTV on the table.**


Kitsch is a good reminder of how much room there is to improve beauty retention. They[cut subscription churn 45% in 12 months](https://skio.com/case-studies/kitsch-cut-churn-in-half-and-doubled-subscribers-with-skio) after moving to Skio.


## Volume discounts solve the beauty-specific churn problem


Volume discounts change the incentive. Instead of rewarding the act of subscribing, they reward building a bigger routine with your brand.


-


**They give hyper-loyal customers a reason to expand.** The subscriber who only buys your serum has a concrete reason to add the cleanser.


-


**They give experimenters a reason to consolidate.** The customer trying everything under the sun gets a better deal by trying more of your line in one order.


-


**They lower shipping cost per item.** Shipping four items to one customer costs far less than shipping one item to four customers.


Multi-product subscribers tend to churn less than single-product subscribers, because their relationship with your brand doesn’t hinge on a single SKU. Your own cohort data will show you how big that gap is. Pull retention by number of products per subscription in Skio Analytics before you build anything.


**Volume discounts encourage customers to add more SKUs per subscription, and multi-product subscribers churn less than single-product subscribers.** Skio’s[volume discounts](https://help.skio.com/docs/volume-discounts) apply automatically at checkout and on recurring orders, so the incentive keeps working after the first order.


## How to structure volume discounts without destroying margins


This is where most brands get nervous, and where most of them are guessing. An operator we spoke with described the root problem.


> The brand doesn’t know their true COGS. So, like, a lot of times, they’re guessing on their COGS. If they knew, like, true cogs, like, almost like real time cogs, dude, then he can just really, like, grow the **** out of that business.


So start there.


1.


**Find your true COGS.** Include product cost, packaging, pick and pack, and payment processing. Use a real number for each SKU.


2.


**Calculate profit per order at each tier.** Profit per order equals cart value times one minus the discount, minus COGS, minus shipping and fulfillment. Run it for a single-item cart and for a cart at each threshold.


3.


**Set thresholds on cart value.** A structure like 10% off at $50, 15% off at $100, and 20% off at $150 or more is a sensible starting point.


4.


**Test discount depth against LTV.** A deeper discount that meaningfully improves retention can be far more profitable than a shallow one that doesn’t.


**Set volume discount thresholds based on cart value, such as $50, $100, and $150, rather than item count, and use true COGS to confirm every tier stays profitable.**


Cart value beats item count for beauty specifically. **Price-based volume discounts work better than quantity-based for beauty because product prices vary widely.** A $45 serum and an $18 mask are not the same unit, and a “buy 3” rule treats them as if they were. Skio supports both, and the[price-based volume discounts](https://help.skio.com/docs/price-based-volume-discounts) guide walks through setup. For a deeper comparison, read[price-based vs. quantity-based volume discounts](https://skio.com/blog/volume-discounts-cart-based-vs-quantity-based) .

## How to communicate volume discounts without confusing customers


A discount nobody sees doesn’t change behavior. Make the tiers impossible to miss.


-


**Show tiers on product pages.** Display the thresholds before checkout so customers can plan their cart.


-


**Nudge in the portal.** Use[portal banners](https://help.skio.com/docs/configuring-customer-portal-experience-settings) to tell subscribers how close they are to the next tier, such as “Add $12 more to unlock 15% off.”


-


**Use your notifications.** Pre-order emails are a natural place for “You’re $8 away from 20% off your next order.”


-


**Be specific in your copy.** “Unlock 20% off at $150+” gives the customer a goal. “Save more when you subscribe to more” gives them nothing to aim for.


**Show volume discount tiers on product pages and nudge customers toward the next threshold in the portal to grow basket size without friction.**

## How to test volume discounts without blowing up your business


1.


**Start with new subscribers only.** Retroactively changing pricing for existing subscribers creates churn risk. Keep your current base on their current terms.


2.


**Test one threshold first.** “Spend $100, get 15% off” is a clean first test. Measure AOV and margin impact before you add more tiers.


3.


**Give it 60-90 days.** AOV moves right away. Churn takes longer to show up in cohort data.


4.


**Track the right metrics.** Watch AOV, churn rate, and net margin per subscriber. Revenue alone will lie to you.


5.


**Find your winners.** Use the[Products Dashboard](https://help.skio.com/docs/products-dashboard) to see which SKUs customers add to reach thresholds, then feature those products in your tier messaging.


**Test volume discounts with new subscribers only, starting with one threshold such as $100 for 15% off, and measure for 60-90 days before scaling.**

## FAQ


**How do volume discounts reduce churn for beauty subscriptions?**


They encourage customers to add more SKUs per order. Multi-product subscribers churn less than single-product subscribers because their routine depends on your brand rather than one product.


**Should I use price-based or quantity-based volume discounts for beauty products?**


Price-based works better for most beauty brands because product prices vary widely. A $45 serum and an $18 mask shouldn’t count the same. Set thresholds like $50, $100, and $150.


**Will deeper discounts destroy my margins?**


Not if you structure them with real numbers. Calculate profit per order at each tier using true COGS, shipping, and fulfillment. Bigger carts spread fixed costs across more product, which is why tiered discounts can raise profit per order.


**Can I apply volume discounts to existing subscribers or only new ones?**


Start with new subscribers only. Changing pricing for existing subscribers creates churn risk. Test, measure, then expand.


**How long does it take to see LTV impact from volume discounts?**


Plan for 60-90 days at minimum. You’ll see AOV lift right away, but churn reduction takes time to show up in cohort data.


**Do volume discounts work with Shopify’s native checkout?**
